Oracle database found
 Potential 8
FilePosition
pom.xmlLine 52
docker-compose.ymlLine 34
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 3
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 12
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 6
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 15

Explanation

Oracle database found. To migrate a Java application that uses an Oracle database to Azure, you can follow these recommendations:

* Migrate to Azure Database for PostgreSQL: Azure recommends migrating Oracle databases to Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server as it provides better cost-effectiveness and performance. Create a managed PostgreSQL Flexible Server database in Azure and choose the appropriate pricing tier based on your application's requirements.

* Use migration tools: Utilize the Azure Database Migration Service (DMS) or third-party tools to migrate your Oracle database schema and data to PostgreSQL. Consider using ora2pg or similar tools to convert Oracle-specific SQL to PostgreSQL-compatible SQL.

* Update database drivers and connection strings: Replace Oracle JDBC drivers with PostgreSQL drivers in your Java application. Update connection strings from Oracle format (jdbc:oracle:thin:) to PostgreSQL format (jdbc:postgresql:).

* Review and convert Oracle-specific code: Identify and convert Oracle-specific SQL functions, stored procedures, and PL/SQL code to PostgreSQL equivalents. Pay attention to data types, syntax differences, and built-in functions.

* Enable monitoring and diagnostics: Utilize Azure Monitor to gain insights into the performance and health of your Java application and the underlying PostgreSQL database. Set up metrics, alerts, and log analytics to proactively identify and resolve issues.

* Implement security measures: Apply security best practices to protect your Java application and the PostgreSQL database. This includes implementing authentication and authorization mechanisms with passwordless connections and leveraging Microsoft Defender for Cloud for threat detection and vulnerability assessments.

* Backup your data: Azure Database for PostgreSQL provides automated backups by default. You can configure the retention period for backups based on your requirements. You can also enable geo-redundant backups, if needed, to enhance data durability and availability.
Password found in configuration file
 Potential 3
FilePosition
src/test/resources/application-test.propertiesLine 5
src/test/resources/application-test.propertiesLine 23
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 5
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 14

Explanation

Using clear passwords in property files is a security risk, as they can be easily compromised if the files are accessed by unauthorized individuals. To enhance the security of your application, it is recommended to employ secure credential management practices.

* Azure Key Vault: Utilize Azure Key Vault to securely store and manage your application's passwords and other sensitive credentials. Azure Key Vault provides a centralized and highly secure location for storing secrets, keys, and certificates.

* Passwordless connections: You can provide an additional layer of security and convenience for accessing resources in Azure by eliminating the need for passwords. This way you can reduce the risk of password-related vulnerabilities, such as weak passwords or password theft.
Restricted configurations found
 Potential 2
FilePosition
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 25
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 2

Explanation

The application uses restricted configurations for Azure Container Apps.
These properties can be automatically injected into your application environment by Azure Container Apps to access managed Config Server and managed Eureka Server.
Please remove them from your application, including configuration files, config server files, command line parameters, Java system attributes, and environment variables.

If configured in configuration files: they will be ignored and overrided by Azure Container Apps.

If configured in Config Server files, command line parameters, Java system attribute, environment variable: they need to be removed or you might experience conflicts and unexpected behavior.

Detects usage of Jakarta Persistence (JPA) APIs
 Potential 5
FilePosition
pom.xmlLine 46

Explanation

The application depends on Jakarta Persistence (JPA) APIs (jakarta.persistence. or legacy javax.persistence.), which are used for object-relational mapping (ORM) and database interaction in Jakarta EE or Java EE applications.

When migrating to Azure:

  • Ensure that the database connection, JPA provider (e.g., Hibernate, EclipseLink), and dialect are compatible with your target Azure database service.
  • Recommended database services include Azure Database for PostgreSQL, Azure Database for MySQL, or Azure SQL Database.
  • For containerized deployments, these JPA-based applications can run on Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) or Azure App Service for Linux/Windows.
  • If using Spring Data JPA, verify that connection pool settings and environment variables are properly configured for the cloud environment.
  • Consider leveraging Azure Key Vault for secure storage of database credentials and connection strings.

Explanation

The application is using a Spring Boot version that is not the latest stable release.
Upgrading to the latest stable version ensures you benefit from the newest features, performance improvements, bug fixes, and security patches. Here are some steps you can take to update your application to the latest stable version of Spring Boot:

  • Choose the latest stable Spring Boot version: Check out Spring Boot Support Versions and identify the latest stable release.
  • Update Spring Boot version: Update the Spring Boot version of your application. There are automated tools like Rewrite to help you with the migration.
  • Address code compatibility: Review your application's codebase for any potential compatibility issues with the target Spring Boot version. Update deprecated APIs or features, address any language or library changes, and ensure that your code follows best practices and standards.
  • Test thoroughly: Execute a comprehensive testing process to verify the compatibility and functionality of your application with the new Spring Boot version. Perform unit tests, integration tests, and system tests to validate that all components and dependencies work as expected.

Architecture Diagram

Photo Album is a single-module Java web application providing a public gallery, photo detail navigation, and authenticated upload and deletion. This static assessment covers /home/runner/work/PhotoAlbum-Java-Lite/PhotoAlbum-Java-Lite; diagrams describe checked-in implementation and container configuration, not a verified running deployment. Credential values are omitted.

Data Storage & External Services

Oracle is the only identified application datastore. The Photo entity maps to photos, storing UUID identifiers, original filenames, MIME types, upload timestamps, dimensions, file sizes, and image bytes through a JPA LOB field. Uploads are saved to the database and /photo/{id} returns those bytes; the bundled file under static/uploads is not evidence of an active filesystem upload pipeline. Repository native queries use Oracle constructs including NVL, ROWNUM, SYSDATE, and DUAL.

Compose deploys the app and Oracle on photoalbum-network, persists Oracle files in oracle_data, and mounts initialization scripts into the database container. App startup depends on the database health check. Database and administrator passwords are supplied through external configuration; no credential values are reproduced here. Bootstrap assets are requested directly by browsers from jsDelivr over HTTPS. No application cache, message broker, object storage, or server-side third-party API integration was identified.

Significant caveats: Both default and Docker profiles set spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=create, so application startup can recreate the schema even when the Oracle volume persists. The configured application endpoint is HTTP; no TLS termination component is present in the examined deployment files. Upload and delete POSTs require authentication, while reads are public; CSRF protection is explicitly disabled. These are configuration observations, not runtime or security-test results. The browser upload script has no explicit login or Authorization-header flow, so authenticated browser upload behavior was not established. The max-files-per-upload setting exists, but no corresponding server-side count enforcement was found in the upload controller/service. No builds, tests, dependency resolution, database connections, or Mermaid renderer were run.

Key Architectural Decisions

  • A layered monolith uses constructor-injected MVC controllers, a PhotoService interface and transactional implementation, and a Spring Data repository; communication within the process is synchronous.
  • Photo content and metadata share Oracle persistence rather than a separate file or object store. Native SQL makes chronological navigation and gallery queries Oracle-specific.
  • Public browsing is separated from authenticated mutation through a configured security filter chain and an externally configured, BCrypt-encoded in-memory administrator; browser presentation combines server-rendered pages and asynchronous upload JSON.

API & Service Communication Contracts

Five application-defined HTTP endpoints serve gallery/detail HTML, accept multipart uploads, delete photos, and return image bytes. Browser requests, in-process service calls, and database operations follow synchronous request/response flows; no backend messaging or remote business-service API was found.

API Endpoints Inventory

All paths are unversioned and belong to photoalbum-java-app. Status codes below distinguish explicit controller behavior from conventional framework behavior.

Service / controllerMethodPathRequest TypeResponse Type
Application / HomeControllerGET/No body or declared query parameters200 HTML index view, with List and cache-busting timestamp in the template model. Retrieval exceptions produce the same view with an empty list, not an explicit error status.
Application / HomeControllerPOST/uploadmultipart/form-data; repeated required files parts bound to List; HTTP Basic authentication required200 JSON Map with success, uploadedPhotos, failedUploads, including partial or total per-file failure. Explicit 400 JSON for an empty list or controller-handled MultipartException; missing required parts are framework binding errors. Unauthenticated requests receive a Basic-auth 401 challenge. Unhandled service/transaction errors can produce framework 5xx responses.
Application / DetailControllerGET/detail/{id}String path ID200 HTML detail view with Photo and adjacent photo IDs; missing/blank ID or caught lookup/navigation error redirects to / (normally 302), rather than returning 404.
Application / DetailControllerPOST/detail/{id}/deleteString path ID; no declared request body; HTTP Basic authentication requiredRedirect to / (normally 302) with success/error flash attributes. Missing photo and caught deletion failures also redirect; no JSON deletion result or explicit 404. Unauthenticated requests receive 401.
Application / PhotoFileControllerGET/photo/{id}String path ID; browser may append an undeclared _t cache-busting query parameter200 ResponseEntity backed by ByteArrayResource, using the stored MIME type; 404 for a missing photo or missing/empty image bytes; 500 for caught exceptions.

Image responses set Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate, private, Pragma: no-cache, Expires: 0, and X-Photo-ID, X-Photo-Name, X-Photo-Size. They do not set a download attachment disposition.

The configured multipart envelope is 10 MB per file and 50 MB per request. Service-level file rejection is represented in the 200 response's failed-upload entries, not generally as HTTP 400. Multipart parsing failures can be mapped to 400 by the local handler; rejection before controller handling may have framework/container-dependent behavior. Detailed validation belongs in business-workflows.md.

Communication Patterns

  • Browser to application: HTML navigation and form submission use HTTP; JavaScript uses asynchronous fetch('/upload') with multipart data and awaits a JSON response. This is asynchronous browser programming, not queue-based backend communication. Images are fetched separately by ID.
  • Within the application: Controllers invoke PhotoService directly; PhotoServiceImpl invokes PhotoRepository synchronously through Spring Data JPA/JDBC. Uploads are processed sequentially, each successful upload followed by an ID lookup to construct response metadata. Detail rendering looks up the selected photo and its older/newer neighbors. These are in-process composition operations, not gateway aggregation.
  • External dependencies: Database calls target the configured Oracle listener; Compose uses the oracle-db hostname via container DNS, not service registration. Templates also direct browsers to fetch Bootstrap CSS/JavaScript over HTTPS from jsDelivr; this is a browser-side asset dependency, not a server-to-server API.
  • Asynchronous backend communication: No message broker, event bus, pub/sub, gRPC, Feign, REST client, or remote business-service call was found.
  • Resilience and timeouts: No application retry, circuit breaker, bulkhead, downstream fallback client, client-side load balancer, or explicit application/database-call timeout was found. No numeric request timeout is therefore asserted. Compose container restart behavior is not an HTTP retry policy. Deployment health-check timing is outside this contract; see configuration-inventory.md.
  • Failure behavior: Gallery load failures become an empty gallery. Detail failures redirect to the gallery; deletion failures redirect with flash feedback. Image-serving exceptions return 500. Upload service validation/read/save failures usually become UploadResult failures and are included in a 200 batch response; a transaction-boundary exception or post-save lookup failure can still escape the controller. A successful save followed by an empty lookup is omitted from both result lists. There is no documented atomic batch or idempotency-key contract.
  • Availability: API availability depends on database access and required credentials at startup; Compose starts the application after database health. No startup ordering among application services exists. Refer to configuration-inventory.md for full dependency/readiness details.
  • Authentication and authorization: Spring Security enforces stateless HTTP Basic authentication for POST /upload and /detail/*/delete; other requests are permitted without authentication. The configured in-memory user has an admin role, but endpoint rules check authentication, not a role. No JWT/OAuth, method-level authorization, ownership checks, or custom login endpoint was found. CSRF protection is disabled. Credentials are externally supplied; their values are intentionally omitted.
  • Transport security: Application configuration and Compose expose HTTP, with no application TLS termination or HTTPS enforcement found. Basic credentials therefore require an external HTTPS boundary for secure transport; no such boundary is established by the checked-in deployment. No explicit JDBC TLS configuration was found. Browser CDN traffic uses HTTPS independently.

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:28-59, service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:52-229, controller sources, src/main/resources/templates/{index,detail,layout}.html, docker-compose.yml.

Startup Dependency Chain

  1. Compose configuration → required credential inputs. Compose required-value interpolation checks ORACLE_PASSWORD, APP_USER_PASSWORD, and APP_ADMIN_PASSWORD before container startup.
  2. oracle-db → Oracle initialization → mounted startup scripts. Initialization scripts require ORACLE_PWD, APP_USER, and APP_USER_PASSWORD. 01-create-user.sh and create-user.sh perform overlapping schema-account initialization. The latter adds a fixed 30-second delay, not an active readiness loop. Actual image script execution behavior was not exercised.
  3. oracle-db health check → successful application-account SQL connection. Compose pipes a simple SQL statement into SQL*Plus using APP_USER and APP_USER_PASSWORD, targeting the local database service XE. Interval: 30s; timeout: 10s; retries: 15; start period: 180s. This verifies a database connection rather than full application readiness.
  4. photoalbum-java-app → waits for healthy oracle-db. Compose declares depends_on: oracle-db: condition: service_healthy, then launches the Java process. Required datasource/admin properties must also resolve for application startup.
  5. Application readiness → not explicitly modeled. No application container health check, readiness probe, config-server retry, discovery dependency, or custom startup timeout was found. No health URL is listed because none is explicitly configured.

The standalone SQL health-check file is not referenced by the Compose health-check command. Compose startup ordering does not establish continuous dependency recovery after the application has started.

Secrets Provisioning Workflow

  1. Operator copies .env.example to the ignored .env or provides the named variables through the invoking shell. Example values are not reproduced or treated as approved credentials.
  2. Compose validates required password inputs and passes database credentials into the database container. The same schema-account names bind to application datasource environment variables. Administrative application credentials bind separately to Spring security properties.
  3. Database startup scripts authenticate through SQL*Plus and create the schema account if absent. The primary script grants CREATE SESSION, CREATE TABLE, CREATE SEQUENCE, CREATE VIEW, CREATE PROCEDURE, CREATE TRIGGER, CREATE TYPE, and CREATE SYNONYM; the additional script grants the first three. No DBA grant appears in these scripts.
  4. Spring resolves datasource credentials and builds an in-memory administrative identity; SecurityConfig encodes the password using BCrypt. Runtime password hashing is not encryption of environment files or container environment values.
  5. Existing-user branches do not rotate an existing schema password. Changing environment inputs alone is not an evidenced password-rotation workflow for a persisted database volume.

No managed identity, service principal, RBAC secret-store binding, encrypted property mechanism, Docker secret mount, or CI secret-retrieval workflow was found. Secrets are exposed to the application through environment values rather than a dedicated secret store. SQL*Plus invocation uses credentials at process invocation; values are intentionally not reproduced. Git ignore rules protect against ordinary accidental staging, not filesystem access or container inspection.

Significant caveats: database property files have no password fallback and Java security configuration requires app.admin.password; local startup outside Compose needs equivalent property provisioning. Several username fallbacks and test/example credential literals exist; none are reproduced. The verification SQL uses literal account selectors rather than the APP_USER binding, so customizing that identity may make its output misleading. The two schema initialization scripts overlap and only create accounts when absent.

Core Business Workflows

Photo Album provides a shared gallery where visitors browse uploaded photographs and navigate between images. Authenticated operators can upload batches of photographs and permanently remove individual photographs.

Assessment workspace: /home/runner/work/PhotoAlbum-Java-Lite/PhotoAlbum-Java-Lite. Findings describe source behavior, not runtime verification; no tests were run. Credential values are intentionally omitted.

Domain Entities

EntityService / Bounded ContextDescriptionKey Relationships
PhotoPhotoService / Photo ManagementAn uploaded photograph, its original content, and information used to display and navigate it. The only persisted business entity found.Independent photograph in a shared gallery; older and newer neighbors are derived by upload time, not explicit relationships.
UploadResult (operation result, not a persisted entity)PhotoService / Upload ProcessingReports whether an individual upload succeeded, its resulting photo reference, or a failure reason.One result per submitted file; successful results refer to a Photo.

There is no Album, customer, owner, or persisted user entity in the examined application model. The gallery is a view over Photos, not a separate aggregate. The configured operator identity belongs to access control, not photo ownership.

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:19-91; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:58-97.

Service-to-Domain Mapping

This is one application with an internal service layer, not independently deployed domain services.

ServiceDomain ContextOwned EntitiesExternal Dependencies
Photo Album application — PhotoServiceImplPhoto Management: upload, discovery, navigation, removalPhoto; produces UploadResultPhotoRepository and the configured relational database, including stored image content
HomeController, DetailController, PhotoFileController (entry-point components, not separate services)Gallery presentation and operator actionsNo independent domain ownership; use PhotoServiceBrowser; shared in-process PhotoService

PhotoService is the business operation boundary; PhotoRepository accesses the source-of-truth Photo records. Controllers compose presentation responses, while browser code combines upload results with image requests. No inter-domain events, backend service calls, or shared ownership between services were found.

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:27-47; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java:15-16.

Primary Workflows

Workflow 1: Upload a batch and update the gallery

  1. An operator selects or drops files in the gallery. Browser upload validation filters files before submission and displays progress.
  2. The browser submits accepted files to POST /upload; the authentication rule gates state-changing access.
  3. HomeController applies the batch-presence rule and calls PhotoService once per file, sequentially.
  4. PhotoService applies upload eligibility and image-dimension rules. It reads the original bytes, attempts dimension extraction, constructs a Photo, and saves content and metadata together.
  5. For each successful result, the controller re-reads the Photo to assemble gallery metadata. Failed results become filename-and-error entries.
  6. The controller returns both result lists. The browser prepends successful photo cards and displays failed-upload messages; each card retrieves its image separately.

The batch permits partial success; there is no all-or-nothing batch transaction or rollback of earlier successful files. A re-read exception is not caught by the upload controller, so it can abort response assembly after some files have already persisted. A successful save whose re-read returns empty is omitted from both result lists.

Evidence: src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:60-159; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:56-107; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:81-184.

Workflow 2: Browse the gallery and navigate photographs

  1. A visitor opens GET /. HomeController obtains the gallery through PhotoService and renders newest-first photo cards.
  2. If loading fails, the controller still renders the gallery with an empty collection. The template presents its normal “No photos yet” message, so an unavailable gallery is indistinguishable from a genuinely empty one.
  3. A visitor opens GET /detail/{id}. DetailController checks the identifier, loads the Photo, and separately obtains older and newer neighbors using the navigation rule.
  4. The page combines the current Photo with neighboring photo references; navigation controls are shown only when the relevant reference exists.
  5. The browser requests GET /photo/{id} to receive stored original content. Missing identifiers, missing records, or missing content return not found; serving exceptions return an error response.

An invalid or missing detail record, or any exception during detail or neighbor lookup, redirects to the gallery rather than rendering a partial detail view. Image responses prevent caching so visitors request current content; no resized thumbnail or image transformation workflow was found.

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:38-50; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:32-58; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:37-86; src/main/resources/templates/index.html:81-113; src/main/resources/templates/detail.html:62-132.

Workflow 3: Delete a photograph

  1. The detail page asks the operator for browser confirmation; cancellation submits nothing.
  2. Confirmation submits POST /detail/{id}/delete, subject to authentication.
  3. PhotoService looks up the Photo. If absent it returns false; otherwise it deletes the record, including its stored content.
  4. DetailController sets a success, not-found, or failure flash message and redirects to the gallery.

This is permanent removal rather than a soft-delete lifecycle. Browser confirmation is a presentation safeguard, not a server-side business precondition.

Evidence: src/main/resources/templates/detail.html:50-59; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:64-78; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:190-208.

No application-level scheduled business jobs, event consumers, batch commands, or startup business-state initialization were found in the examined application sources. The startup class only launches the application.

Cross-Service Data Flows

There are no backend cross-service composition flows, gateways, message brokers, or circuit breakers in the examined implementation.

  • Upload composition: browser files → HomeController → PhotoService → PhotoRepository → database. HomeController joins each successful upload result to a fresh Photo lookup by photo ID, returning metadata; the browser subsequently retrieves image content by that ID.
  • Detail composition: DetailController combines the selected Photo with older/newer Photo references from separate calls in the same domain. The browser then retrieves the selected image independently.
  • Source of truth: the same Photo record supplies gallery metadata and image content; no remote object-storage handoff is implemented in the examined service.
  • Degradation: gallery lookup failure becomes an empty page; detail lookup/navigation failure redirects home; image content failure becomes not-found or server error. No stale-data fallback exists. Upload validation failures remain per-file results, but controller re-read failures and transaction-completion failures can escape that result handling.

These are internal orchestration and browser-to-application flows, not choreography or distributed transactions.

Business Workflow Sequence

sequenceDiagram actor Operator participant Browser as "Gallery browser" participant Access as "Access control" participant Home as "Upload controller" participant Service as "Photo service" participant Photo as "Photo entity" participant Store as "Photo repository and database" Operator->>Browser: Select or drop photographs Browser->>Browser: Apply browser upload validation Browser->>Access: Submit accepted photographs alt Not authenticated Access-->>Browser: Authentication required Browser-->>Operator: Upload failed else Authenticated Access->>Home: Process batch loop Each submitted file Home->>Service: Upload photograph Service->>Service: Apply upload eligibility and dimension rules alt Rejected or file reading fails Service-->>Home: Failed file and reason else Eligible Note over Service: Missing dimension reader does not block storage Service->>Photo: Create photograph with original content Service->>Store: Save photograph alt Save call succeeds Store-->>Service: Saved photograph Service-->>Home: Successful photo reference Home->>Service: Retrieve saved photograph for gallery Service->>Store: Find photograph by reference Store-->>Service: Photograph Service-->>Home: Gallery metadata else Save call throws Service-->>Home: Failed file and storage error end end end Home-->>Browser: Successful photographs and failed files Browser-->>Operator: New photo cards and failure feedback end

The normal per-file outcomes are shown above. A transaction-completion or controller re-read exception can interrupt this response path after earlier files have persisted; no compensating batch action is implemented.

Business Rules & Decision Logic

Validation and eligibility

  • Batch presence: no files produces a bad-request response. Multipart exceptions handled by HomeController also produce “No files provided,” even when the underlying multipart failure has another cause.
  • Browser upload validation: accepts JPEG, PNG, GIF, and WebP MIME types and files no larger than 10 MiB. It is a client convenience, not authoritative enforcement.
  • Server upload eligibility: lowercases the submitted MIME type and checks the configured allowlist; rejects files above the configured byte limit and files with nonpositive length. Examined configurations allow the same four MIME types and set a 10 MiB file limit; multipart limits additionally bound a whole request to 50 MB as configured.
  • Batch-count caveat: configuration declares app.file-upload.max-files-per-upload=10, but no application enforcement was found in the upload controller, service, or browser code.
  • Image-dimension rule: when an image reader is available, dimensions from the first image header must not exceed 40,000,000 pixels in total. An I/O exception rejects the file; no suitable reader, or a non-I/O extraction exception, allows continuation without dimensions. The implementation does not require a successful full image decode or establish agreement between declared MIME type and actual content.
  • Photo model constraints: original filename must be nonblank and at most 255 characters; MIME type must be nonblank and at most 50 characters; size must be present and positive; upload time must be present. These are declared entity validation constraints, not explicit controller request validation. Image content and dimensions are not required by equivalent model validation annotations.
  • A missing submitted MIME type reaches the service's generic failure handling rather than a dedicated validation message.

Evidence: src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:60-79; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:33-34,85-180; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:31-75; src/main/resources/application.properties:24-30; src/main/resources/application-docker.properties:20-27.

Ordering, lifecycle, and computed information

  • Navigation rule: the previous image is the most recent strictly older upload; the next is the earliest strictly newer upload, additionally bounded by database current time. Equal upload timestamps are not neighbors under these comparisons. Gallery ordering has no explicit tie-breaker.
  • Photo creation: construction generates a new photo reference and current application upload time. Re-uploading the same filename or content creates another Photo; no duplicate-content or filename uniqueness rule was found.
  • Lifecycle: submitted file → rejected with no new Photo, or persisted Photo → permanently deleted Photo. No approval, publication, archival, restoration, or ownership-transfer states were found.
  • Derived presentation: gallery cards display rounded kilobytes and optional dimensions; detail views format size and upload time. Neighbor references are calculated at request time, not maintained as domain relationships.
  • No bidirectional domain relationships need synchronization in the examined model.

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:78-90; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java:23-62; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:190-229; src/main/resources/templates/detail.html:104-132.

Transactions, errors, audit, and authorization

  • Transactions: PhotoServiceImpl is transactional; query methods explicitly use read-only transactions. Controller calls are separate transaction boundaries, so a batch and detail composition are not one consistent unit of work. Success returned inside a service method is not proof of transaction completion: deferred persistence or commit failures may escape the method's internal catch blocks.
  • Errors: upload service failures generally become UploadResult messages. Gallery and detail controllers degrade as described above; delete failures become flash messages; content-serving failures become error responses. No retries, durable compensation, dead-letter handling, or business-specific exception hierarchy was found.
  • Logging: uploads, rejections, deletion, retrieval failures, and image-serving activity are logged. Image serving also logs filenames and a prefix of image bytes. No durable business audit history or actor-linked change record was found.
  • Authorization: upload and delete POST requests require authentication using stateless HTTP Basic. Although the configured identity is assigned an ADMIN role, these route checks require authentication, not an explicit role. Reads are public; there are no per-photo ownership rules. CSRF protection is disabled.
  • Operator experience caveat: public templates expose upload and delete controls without authentication-aware visibility, and the upload JavaScript has no dedicated login flow; unsuccessful HTTP responses receive generic upload feedback.

Data Architecture & Persistence Layer

The data layer contains one JPA entity, Photo, persisted through Spring Data JPA/Hibernate to Oracle, with H2 configured for tests. Photo metadata and original image bytes reside together in the photos table.

  • Non-unique index idx_photos_uploaded_at covers upload time. No foreign keys, associations, cascade mappings, bidirectional links, join tables, or optimistic-lock version field are declared. Consequently the diagram intentionally contains no relationship edges.
  • UploadResult (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/UploadResult.java:6-10) is a non-persisted result DTO, not an entity or separate table.
  • PhotoServiceImpl has class-level @Transactional; retrieval/list/navigation methods override it with read-only transactions (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:27-29,53-54,67-68,216-229). Upload and deletion use the class-level transaction. Upload catches persistence exceptions; a successful result assembled before transaction completion is not proof of a committed write.
  • All custom repository queries select the binary column as well as metadata. The gallery query is unbounded, so metadata listings can materialize image bytes for every returned photo; no metadata-only projection or streaming BLOB API is declared.

Key Repository Methods

Repository source: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java:15-62. PhotoRepository extends JpaRepository; inherited CRUD methods are omitted below.

ServiceRepositoryNotable MethodsPurpose
Photo AlbumPhotoRepositoryList findAllOrderByUploadedAtDesc()Native SQL returns all photos newest-first; Oracle NVL supplies a fallback MIME type. No pagination parameter.
Photo AlbumPhotoRepositoryList findPhotosUploadedBefore(LocalDateTime uploadedAt)Native SQL selects strictly older records in descending time order and limits the outer result to ten rows using Oracle ROWNUM.
Photo AlbumPhotoRepositoryList findPhotosUploadedAfter(LocalDateTime uploadedAt)Native SQL selects strictly newer records in ascending time order, bounded above by Oracle SYSDATE obtained through DUAL; no row-count limit.

No custom batch aggregation finder, stored procedure, cross-service query, or separate JDBC mapper was found. The custom queries depend on Oracle SQL semantics; H2 test configuration does not explicitly enable Oracle compatibility. The existing PhotoAlbumApplicationTests only loads the application context, so it does not establish query portability or exercise repository behavior.

Timestamp-only comparisons have no ID tie-breaker and exclude records sharing the reference timestamp. The newer-record query also couples results to the database clock while upload timestamps originate from the JVM.

Data Ownership Boundaries

One application module owns a single domain table in its configured relational database. There is no evidence of multiple independently owned data services, a database-per-service topology, shared cross-service tables, API-based data aggregation, event/outbox replication, CQRS, or a separate read model. H2 is a test substitute, not an additional production owner.

Reads and writes use the same entity/repository and configured data source. Image bytes are database-owned BLOB content, not references to an object store or runtime filesystem upload store. The existing static JPEG and test upload-path setting do not establish a second active persistence mechanism: the inspected upload service saves image bytes directly to the database.

The entity contains no account, tenant, or owner identifier. Therefore ownership isolation cannot be derived from row-level associations. Application authentication protects state changes, while photo reads are publicly allowed; no per-photo ownership or field-level authorization is implemented in the inspected model/security configuration.

SecurityConfig hashes the externally supplied administrator password with BCrypt for its in-memory authentication record; that is not encryption of photo data. Database/admin credential values are intentionally omitted or marked [REDACTED] throughout this document.

PhotoServiceImpl logs original filenames, and PhotoFileController.java:53-66,71-82 logs filenames and a short image-byte prefix and returns filename metadata in response headers. No masking/redaction control for these photo-derived values was found.

Assessment limitations: static source/configuration inspection only; no database connection, tests, builds, or live schema inspection performed. Deployed schema, effective pool settings, external encryption/backup/retention controls, actual image sensitivity, and runtime query compatibility remain unverified.
